# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Critical Reading: "Two Years On," Varden 24-Month Follow-up and Halden Subset

This is a strong follow-up. It does what the earlier critiques asked for:

- **Better hours measure:** system-log hours, to catch work not claimed on timesheets.
- **Registered test of the meetings idea,** filed before the 24-month outcomes existed.
- **Baseline meeting data,** which answers my earlier concern that the 9-month comparison was cross-sectional. Treated and control offices started at 7.4 and 7.2 hours a week.
- **Waiting times against a control group:** 7.3 minutes in treated counter offices against 4.0 in control.
- **Honest framing of the Halden subset** as survivors with no comparison group.

The arithmetic checks out:

- **Timesheets:** 0.966 ÷ 0.88 gives +9.8% per hour.
- **System logs:** 0.966 ÷ 0.89 gives +8.5%.
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9 ÷ 40.3 is −13.4%, and 96.8 ÷ 0.866 gives +11.8%.
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- **Counter staffing:** the 12% figure fits the 9-month results. Each employee worked 17% fewer hours but handled 6.7% more per hour, so restoring output needs about 1 ÷ 0.886, or roughly 13%, more staff.

Its corrections to Varga & Holm and to the meta-analysis are largely justified. The weak points are an overlooked control-group contamination that muddies the decay estimate, some loose wording in the Summary, and a mediation result that is less independent and less behavioural than "confirms" suggests.

## Problems

### 1. Control offices changed their practice, and the decay estimate doesn't allow for it

From month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their own meetings and raised their output per hour by about 4.1%. The paper reports this as a hint that reorganisation alone might capture some of the gain. It doesn't note what it does to the main estimate.

When control offices improve, the gap between treated and control narrows even if treated offices haven't changed. Roughly, two of seven offices improving by 4.1% lifts the control average by about 1.2 points. That could account for close to half of the like-for-like decline from 12.5% to 9.8%.

So the "fading" may partly reflect the control group catching up, quite possibly because they learned from treated offices in the same county. The paper should show the 24-month estimate with those two offices excluded, or analyse it with their change taken into account.

### 2. The Summary compares two different hours measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." The 12.5% uses timesheets and the 8.5% uses system logs. The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% to 9.8%, a fall of about a fifth, not a third. Section 5's "about a quarter" is closer.

The confidence intervals also overlap heavily (+6.9 to +18.4 at nine months, +4.6 to +15.2 at 24 months), and no test of the difference is reported. With only two time points, the data can't show whether the gain has levelled off or is still falling. "Declined but not disappeared" is fair for month 24 only.

### 3. The mediation result is weaker than "confirms" suggests

- **Same offices, not a replication.** The test was registered at month 11, after the exploratory finding, in the same 14 offices that produced it. The outcome data after month 11 were new, so this is a genuine prospective test. But it is not independent confirmation. "Survives" in the body is the right word; "confirms" in the Summary is not.
- **Office-months don't add independent clusters.** The effective sample is still 14 offices, so the problem I raised about cluster-robust intervals with few clusters still applies. The 28–66% interval may be too narrow.
- **The two pathways overlap.** Fewer meetings could itself reduce fatigue. How the gain is split between the two depends on how the model orders them, so 47% and 18% are not cleanly separable shares. The authors acknowledge the general confounding assumption but not this specific problem.

### 4. It's unclear what the log hours measure, and the meetings pathway may partly be arithmetic

"Active log-in time on the case-management system" is described as time "working on cases." If it counts only case-system time, it excludes meetings. Then it doesn't measure the same thing as total hours, and the meaning of "output per log-measured hour" changes.

Either way, cutting meetings raises output per *total* hour largely by definition, because time moves from meetings, which produce no cases, to case work. That is still useful to know: it says the gain comes from *how time is spent* more than from *working faster*. But it is closer to accounting than to behavioural change. The paper should say exactly what the log measure captures and whether meeting time is inside or outside it.

### 5. Case-processing still has no timeliness measure

At 24 months the paper still reports no backlog size, time-to-decision or deadline compliance for case-processing, the outcome I flagged at nine months. The original Limitations section named backlog growth as a risk. Appeal overturns also remain a raw treated-versus-control comparison (3.2% v 3.0%), not a difference-in-differences estimate with an interval, and the gap has widened slightly.

### 6. The reversion pattern is messier than the Summary says

One of the three Halden reverters is a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Under the meta-analysis's coding, marketing is discretionary work. The Summary's phrase "client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches the category to fit.

The more useful lesson is that being available to respond to clients is a form of coverage obligation that sector labels miss. That supports the meta-analysis's caveat that the discretionary versus coverage-bound split is a simplification.

### 7. The Halden subset is selected twice, and one author has a stake

- **Who responded:** 14 of the 23 organisations that had records responded, and those 23 were themselves a non-random subset. Organisations that reverted or struggled may have been less willing to take part.
- **The authors' framing:** they call the continuers' +11.8% an "upper bound." It isn't a formal bound. It is an estimate that is probably biased upward. Their caution is right; the term is too precise.
- **Who is reporting:** R. Okafor, lead author of the original Halden paper, is a co-author. The report doesn't acknowledge the misreported timing of the original withdrawals, which the Halden follow-up section is well placed to correct.

### 8. Smaller points

- **Cost per contact:** The county's figure is +9%, but 12% more staff at full pay implies about +12%. The figures reconcile only if staff are about 75% of total cost. The basis should be stated.
- **The month-ten rebuttal:** This compares Varden *output* with a Halden *energy* extrapolation from a different population. It works as a rebuttal of Varga & Holm's general claim, but the two figures don't measure the same thing. As noted before, a straight-line extrapolation would have reached zero at about month 8.7 anyway.
- **What the follow-up confirms about the meta-analysis:** It reveals that all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That confirms my earlier objection to the "no decay" claim.

## What changes in the overall picture

| Question | Before this report | After |
|---|---|---|
| Is there a per-hour gain under strong measurement? | About 8–10%, from overlapping, short studies | Yes, about 8.5–10% at 24 months in one randomised trial with log-measured hours |
| Does it decay? | Open; the meta-analysis's "no decay" was unfounded | Some decline, probably modest, but partly confounded by control offices cutting their own meetings |
| Mechanism | Untested | Fewer meetings is the largest measured pathway, fatigue is smaller, and about a third is unexplained. This comes from the generating sample and is partly arithmetic. |
| Could reorganisation alone deliver the gain? | Not asked | Suggestive but uncontrolled evidence from two offices. This is now the most important open question. |
| Coverage-bound work | About −9% to −11% output, worse service | Confirmed decisively: the county ended the arm, and restoring service would need about 12% more staff |
| Sector labels as a guide | Discretionary vs coverage-bound | Responsiveness obligations, such as client deadlines, also matter |
| Per-employee output, discretionary work | Roughly maintained | Slightly below control (−3.4%, CI includes zero). The hours cut is mostly, not fully, offset. |

The body of evidence now supports a fairly specific conclusion. In backlog-type work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours yields about an 11–13% cut in actual hours and a durable per-hour gain of about 8–10%. Roughly half of that gain comes from removing low-value meeting time, which leaves output per employee a few percent below what it would otherwise be, alongside sustained reductions in sickness and resignations.

The question these studies raise but cannot answer is how much of the gain an employer could get by cutting meetings without cutting hours. Answering it needs a trial with a reorganisation-only arm.
